items.lbText:
For decades, the capital’s house prices raced ahead of the national average – but now they are falling in prime areas

A n elegant Georgian facade, a full-width balcony and an exclusive address in South Kensington just steps from the Natural History Museum and the V&A. Yet the listing price of this west London flat at Queen’s Gate Gardens has dropped by nearly £1m since last year, to £4.4m.

It is far from an isolated case. A nearby house originally listed at £20m was slashed to £14m this year, says a local estate agent. In neighbouring Notting Hill, a stucco-fronted property that came to market two years ago at £16m is now being offered for less than £14m, they said.

London’s premium property market is stuck in a rut. While borrowing costs and stretched affordability weigh on everyday buyers , the city’s richest residents are also making deep cuts to the prices of their multimillion-pound homes.

This market is a world away from the rest of the UK property market – where the average house price was just under £275,000 in September , according to Nationwide. The well-heeled neighbourhoods also present a stark contrast with much of the capital, where Londoners struggle to get on to the housing ladder, face rising rents and a lack of affordable housing, and estate agents report the market for flats is now “dead”.

But neighbourhoods such as Knightsbridge, bordering Hyde Park and home to Harrods, are also feeling the pinch, said Harry Dawes, a buying agent based in Belgravia.

“There is a flat on Pont Street, a five-minute walk from Harrods, which sold at £4.4m in 2014, then sold at £3.5m. It can now be bought at £2.5m.”

For decades, London’s property prices raced ahead of the national average. But that gap has been slowly narrowing: while the average price of a UK home rose by about 2% in the year ended in June, prices in inner London boroughs fell by 8.3%, according to the Office for National Statistics.

That drop has been particularly pronounced in Westminster – which includes areas such as Marylebone, Belgravia and Mayfair – with prices down 25.4% year on year. In the City, prices slumped by 20.4%, and in Kensington and Chelsea, prices fell 14.7%.

Properties in the capital became overvalued in the mid-2010s after a period of rapid price growth, said Anthony Payne, the chief executive of the data analyst LonRes. London was then hit hard by Brexit, the Covid pandemic, higher property taxes and a surge in borrowing costs.

Now, owners who bought at the peak now face losses of as much as 25% if they choose to sell, according to estimates from the estate agent Savills.

“London benefited dramatically from international investment and buyers wanting property here as a store of wealth and a way of making money,” Payne said. “These are the people that inflated the market, but now more and more of them are deserting it.”

Jeremy Gee, the managing director at the super-prime estate agent Beauchamp Estates – whose portfolio includes a £42m sub-penthouse overlooking Hyde Park – said the decline had also been driven partly by the exit of super-wealthy groups from the UK, especially after the abolition of the non-dom tax regime.

“There is a section of society who have left the UK recently for lots of reasons, but mainly because of tax,” he said.

“When there are not that many buyers and lots of properties, the prices are going to be softer. Many of our sellers have decided that enough is enough – let’s just sell the property and move on.”

Tax changes have put sellers on edge, too, he added. Last year, the former chancellor Rachel Reeves announced plans for a “mansion tax” on homes worth more than £2m.

This nervousness has triggered a slowdown across the higher tiers of London’s market. Prime properties spent an average of 186 days on the market in the first half of 2026, up from 178 days in the first half of 2025, according to LonRes. Over the same period, the average discount to asking price widened from 8.3% to 10.4% – sellers have grown more likely to accept lowball offers.

Sellers, who normally own these properties for at least a decade, “don’t like it but have to accept it,” said Dawes.

“If they are older, they have to take a lifetime view on their property and accept that from a profit and loss perspective, this last trade might not look good.

“We bought three flats for a client’s kids last year – two in Chelsea and one in Notting Hill – and every seller was selling at a loss.”

Even with multimillion pound discounts propping up on the market, Stuart Bailey, the head of super-prime London sales at the estate agent Knight Frank, said there were still buyers willing to pay above the asking price for “the very best in class” properties.

“A fabulous address, lovely views, immaculate style and newly refurbished,” he said. “It is a matter of premium or discount, retail or trade, brand new or not, and there is nowhere in between. It’s the discounted properties dragging the market down.

“Sellers are more and more realistic about moving on,” he added. “They do not see material price growth on the horizon.”

“With a Labour government the concern is always that there’s going to be some kind of wealth tax somewhere,” he said.

“But many wealthy people also just accept the cost of taxation and that London is simply an expensive city to live in.”

Camilla Dell, a buying agent, said demand is still strong from a wide base of international buyers, including Americans, Singaporeans and Nigerians. Politics, she said, rarely comes up in conversation.

“Most people accept that the UK does not have the best political stability but they want to live here,” she said. “And actually, it helped that Andy Burnham ruled out an overhaul of property taxes in the next budget.”…

items.lbText:
Climate crisis blamed as virus that originated in Africa spreads to livestock as far north as Aberdeenshire

British farmers are experiencing the worst bluetongue season on record, with the number of cases surpassing the past three years combined.

The viral disease, which affects sheep and cattle among other animals, can cause fevers, ulcers, a swollen head and lameness. The tongue may go blue and even protrude from the mouth. In the most severe cases, the animal can die.

The virus, which is transmitted via biting midges and originated in Africa, has spread to Europe over the past two decades, a development the World Organisation for Animal Health links to climate breakdown. The particular strain of bluetongue currently affecting livestock, serotype 3 (BTV-3), was first found in England in 2023.

Academics have said the transmission is inextricably linked to the temperature of the surrounding environment, with hotter temperatures, caused by the climate crisis, contributing to a rise in cases being recorded farther north.

Bluetongue does not affect people or food safety, but Robyn Munt, the vice-president of the National Farmers’ Union, said farmers were having to keep “constant vigilance” and continually check their livestock for symptoms.

So far in this year’s bluetongue season, which runs from 1 July 2026 to 30 June 2027, Defra has recorded 2,201 cases, 1,103 in September.

Despite being just three months old, the 2026-27 season has already seen more cases than the past three seasons combined.

Defra defines a case as a premises where at least one animal with bluetongue is present, so the total number of animals affected is likely to be higher than the number of reported cases.

Farmers can vaccinate their livestock against the disease but Munt said it had been “really challenging” for them to get hold of the vaccines, as it was a “demand-led process”.

“During a year where livestock businesses, due to the climate impact of drought, have carried a whole load of cost in their business that they might not have been expecting, dealing with vaccinating animals and then potentially having to treat animals with bluetongue is just more labour pressure and stress on a farm business,” she said.

This summer the disease has crossed into Scotland for the first time and has been found as far north as Aberdeenshire.

With temperatures still consistently high enough in many parts of the UK for the virus to develop inside the midges, Tom Cantillon, a senior analyst at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, said this year’s record outbreak was a “harbinger of things to come”.

“With climate change increasing the likelihood of milder winters and hotter summers, pests and pathogens that were once unable to survive here can now make their home. This will profoundly impact not only farmers, but the wider public,” he said.

Earlier this summer mosquitoes capable of transmitting Zika virus and dengue were found breeding in homes in east London, with experts predicting that the rapidly warming climate could lead to greater “incursions of invasive mosquitoes”.

Cantillon said: “Adequate preparation for these pests and pathogens is necessary, including vaccinations for farm animals. But, ultimately, we cannot vaccinate against the kinds of climate that encourage these outbreaks. They will only get more likely until we reduce our emissions to net zero and stop warming altogether.”

The Fed’s inspector general on Wednesday said it found ‌no grounds for a criminal referral or evidence of administrative misconduct tied to the project cost overruns. But its conclusion there was lax oversight drew a fresh call for Powell’s resignation from Donald Trump, who across his two presidencies has been a vociferous critic of Powell.

Powell has remained at ‌the Fed as a governor since stepping down as chair in May.

His successor as Fed chair, Kevin ​Warsh said, on Thursday he would hire an independent auditor to “verify accuracy and compliance” for all of the project’s costs.

Blanche told Bloomberg News that if the new review found any evidence ⁠of criminal wrongdoing, the justice department could investigate.

At his final ​press conference ​as Fed chief in ​April, Powell said he would not leave the ​central bank’s board “until this ‌investigation is well and ​truly over, ​with transparency and finality”.

A Fed spokesperson had no immediate comment on Blanche’s statements.

items.lbText:
Leaders agree a coordinated drawdown after surge in prices and Donald Trump’s threat to cut off US supplies

Leaders of G7 nations are to release up to 100m barrels of their emergency diesel and crude oil stockpiles after Donald Trump threatened to cut off supplies of US diesel.

The French President, Emmanuel Macron , said ministers from some of world’s largest economies had agreed to release stocks from their strategic oil reserves after crisis talks on Friday.

Macron convened the leaders’ video call to discuss the global surge in diesel prices, and Trump’s threat to cut off US diesel exports unless Europe tapped their own stockpiles to help cool global markets.

Under proposals reportedly drawn up by Macron, the current G7 chair, members will release 50m barrels of diesel and 50m of crude oil into the global market to ease prices.

The agreement suggests European countries will avoid being cut off from vital supplies of US diesel after coming under pressure from the White House in recent days to release their emergency supplies or face a US diesel export ban.

Trump said he was considering a ban on diesel exports after the surge in sales to overseas buyers pushed US diesel prices to record highs in a blow to the economy before the US midterm elections in November.

Macron said G7 nations – which also includes the US, UK, Germany, Italy, Canada and Japan – wanted to “work in a coordinated manner to help bring down the prices of petroleum products, particularly diesel”.

He added that the G7 members and partners would front-load a substantial diesel release within the first 20 days and that ministers would discuss the “possibility of additional diesel releases as necessary” in the coming days.

“We have all committed together to releasing these strategic reserves in the proportions I mentioned, with a focus on diesel, and we are all committed to ensuring there are no export bans, and President Trump, in particular, was very clear on this point,” Macron said.

Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Europe had “agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil” and that the process would start “immediately”.

The threat of a US export ban presented a considerable challenge for Europe, which produces about 70% of the diesel it consumes from domestic refineries but relies on imports to make up the shortfall.

The ongoing disruption to fossil fuel exports from the Middle East has limited output from the region’s refineries as well as those in China, which is a leading buyer of Gulf crude. Meanwhile, Russian refineries have come under attack from Ukraine, causing its fuel output to fall to 20-year lows.

In response, the US exported a record high of 1.9m barrels a week to overseas buyers in early August as the slump in global refining squeezed supplies across Europe and Asia.

The record exports caused the US’s own distillate stockpiles to fall to their lowest seasonal levels since 1996, causing diesel pump prices to climb above $5.85 (£4.45) a gallon for the first time in early September.

The proposed ban on US exports was expected to fuel greater competition for cargoes on the global market which would push prices in the UK and Europe well beyond current record levels.

In the UK, the average price of diesel at the pumps climbed to a record high of £2 a litre on forecourts on Friday, putting more pressure on motorists and the wider economy.

The cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, according to the RAC motoring group, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war. UK lorries, vans and farming vehicles are also typically diesel-fuelled, meaning the price rises will be felt in the higher cost of goods across the economy.

Brent crude oil was trading at just above $100 (£76) a barrel on Friday, compared with about $72 before the Iran war started. It fell to about $98 a barrel following news of the emergency stockpile release before returning to more than $102 a barrel by the end of the day.

Macquarie Group’s Walt Chancellor said Europe’s decision to rely more on its own emergency reserves than US imports would not address the underlying problem in the US or the global market.

“The core issue the US faces is not a diesel problem. Nor is it a refined product problem. It may not even be a petroleum problem. It is a global energy problem,” he said, according to CNBC.

“So what is the solution then? In short, more oil through the strait of Hormuz and out of the Middle East. Anything short of that is really just shuffling deck chairs,” he added.

The IEA, the world’s energy watchdog, ordered the largest release of government oil reserves in its history in March when it agreed to release 400m barrels of emergency crude, to help calm the oil price shock sparked by the US-Israeli attacks on Iran.

The intervention represented a third of the group’s total government stockpiles and was more than double the release of 182m barrels of oil made in 2022 after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

items.title: Utilities are public services – and should not be run as businesses | Letters
items.author: Guardian Staff
items.content:
Readers respond to an article by Will Hutton and Andy Haldane suggesting that they could be run for the public benefit

Utilities should not be run as businesses but as essential public services. They do not function in isolation, and business models are unsuited to their functioning in the public interest. They have social and environmental as well as economic responsibilities that have to be met. For 20 years, prior to the advent of the Scottish parliament, local government functioned well in Scotland within a framework of regions and districts. The regions had powers and responsibilities for the wide range of functions that had to be coordinated and operated strategically at the regional level. They included water and sewerage.

Continue reading...
items.lbText:
Readers respond to an article by Will Hutton and Andy Haldane suggesting that they could be run for the public benefit

Will Hutton and Andy Haldane advocate “turning [utilities] into public-benefit companies with a primary, constitutional objective of delivering high-quality services, with profitability subordinate to that broader aim” ( Andy Burnham talks about ‘public control’ of the utilities but it’s a minefield. We can lead him through it, 25 September ). So still companies, but with a public interest rather than a profit motive. This is still the wrong approach.

Utilities should not be run as businesses but as essential public services. They do not function in isolation, and business models are unsuited to their functioning in the public interest. They have social and environmental as well as economic responsibilities that have to be met. For 20 years, prior to the advent of the Scottish parliament, local government functioned well in Scotland within a framework of regions and districts. The regions had powers and responsibilities for the wide range of functions that had to be coordinated and operated strategically at the regional level. They included water and sewerage.

The present government appears to be edging sideways, through metro mayors and joint working, towards governance for city regions. This should be formalised and given a full portfolio of responsibilities, powers and resources for strategic planning, economic development, education, health, transportation, infrastructure and the environment. Infrastructure should include water and sewerage.

As an example, urban rainwater needs to be collected and recycled for cooling, which was normal practice for thousands of years in southern Europe. Such practice should be moving north to include water reserves for wildfire control. How could such provisions, urban cooling and wildfire control ever be met through the profit motive?

If the present water companies in England have liabilities that exceed the value of their assets, and cannot meet their legal responsibilities, then it is difficult to see why they should be rescued and maintained through public expenditure. Roger Read Former secretary general, Metrex

Will Hutton and Andy Haldane put forward a poor argument for maintaining private ownership of utilities. Instead of comparing the present situation with how things were when the water utilities were publicly owned – surely the fairest comparison – they cite spurious examples of the alleged failings of other nationalised industries.

We are alone in the world (apart from Chile) in having a wholly privatised water industry; is everyone else out of step? Sally Thompson Cardiff

Will Hutton and Andy Haldane give some interesting thoughts on the public control of utilities. These could also apply across the complete essential services sector, from water companies to dental practices. Few who experienced the performance of the old postwar nationalised industries would wish a return to this failed model. However, why not just keep it simple and legislate to force all essential-services operators to list as companies on the London Stock Exchange?

For each sector, further legislation could set maximums for yields and permitted borrowing: two key indicators of company activity. The public would then be more inclined to invest in the companies, just as they do at present with National Grid. Ian Graham Port Carlisle, Cumbria

items.lbText:
Owen Fraser responds to an article by Anna Tims on the price schoolchildren without smartphones pay on buses

I applaud Anna Tims for her article ( Schoolchildren without smartphones penalised with higher bus fares, 26 September ), raising the need for a unified approach on this issue to properly tackle the ill effects of such technology on children in the classroom and beyond.

I live in Scotland , where this issue is addressed by making bus travel free for children and young people under the age of 22 with a physical national entitlement card. I am, however, affected by the more general problem of cheaper bus pass options being hidden behind smartphone apps.

I use a non-standard operating system on my phone owing to the always-online models of Android and iOS, which I prefer to avoid.

When comparing the prices of First’s weekly bus pass in my area, which is available to purchase on the bus, and its monthly pass, which is exclusive to its app, I am spending £264 extra over the course of a year simply for not using a phone that this specific app is designed for.

This is unacceptable even without the issues I raised about the main two mobile operating systems, even more so in the context of the present cost of living generally. Accessible public transport should not depend on which computer software is used by the passenger.

First is far from the only offender in this regard – for instance, many supermarkets’ loyalty schemes are now only available as apps as well. Owen Fraser Aberdeen

A new play about the art-loving Bloomsbury Group member speaks of the enduring battle of ideas with his free-market rival Friedrich Hayek

T he sound of guns from the advancing German armies could be heard clearly by John Maynard Keynes as his train trundled across northern France in the spring of 1918. The evidence of the struggle on the western front was everywhere but Keynes, then a Treasury official, was not heading to Paris on war business; he was off to buy some art.

Keynes made the risky trip to attend an auction of the studio of Edgar Degas, who had died the previous year. The man who would become the foremost economist of the 20th century returned to London with some impressionist treasures for the National Gallery, having successfully petitioned the chancellor of the exchequer to spend £20,000 at the sale.

This story reveals much about Keynes. His skill in lobbying officialdom for funds at a time when the country was involved in a costly war. His love of art, which culminated in him being instrumental in setting up the Arts Council. His conviction that economics mattered less than the good things in life.

All of which makes the title of James Graham’s new play about Keynes, The Standard of Living , wholly appropriate. Keynes pored over statistics but was much more than a number cruncher. He had firm views about why the economy was malfunctioning in the 1920s and 1930s, but was just as interested in discussing philosophy with Bertrand Russell and Ludwig Wittgenstein. He believed a growing economy should provide the opportunity for more leisure time rather than the accumulation of monetary wealth. He revolutionised economics without having a revolutionary bone in his body.

Born into a well-off academic family, Keynes went to Eton before studying maths at Cambridge. His circle of friends after university was the Bloomsbury Group, painters and writers who included Virginia Woolf, and two of his lovers, Lytton Strachey and Duncan Grant. This was a group that prided itself on being unconventional, on not accepting the status quo.

Bloomsbury helped satisfy Keynes’s cultural needs but also helped shape his economic thinking. He did not see growth as an end in itself but rather as a means to live the good life or – as he put it – to live like the “lilies in the field”. In Economic Possibilities for Our Grandchildren he foresaw a time when the economic problem had been solved, when the working week would be considerably shorter and “when the accumulation of wealth was no longer of high social importance”.

His willingness to challenge the orthodoxy was demonstrated in an early book, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, which correctly predicted that the punitive terms imposed by the treaty of Versailles in 1919 would result in a humiliated Germany remaining bitter and vengeful.

To the surprise of his Bloomsbury friends, Keynes later fell in love with a Russian ballet dancer, Lydia Lopokova, and the couple married in 1925 when he was 42. While forthright and confident when expressing his opinions, Keynes was self-conscious about his appearance, considering himself repulsive. Others agreed. Virginia Woolf once described him as like “a gorged seal, double chin, ledge of red lip, little eyes, sensual, brutal, unimaginative”.

One of the central themes of the play is the battle of ideas between Keynes and the Austrian economist Friedrich Hayek. The latter believed that left to their own devices, free markets provided the best economic outcomes and that over the long term crises would be resolved without the need for state intervention.

Keynes took the opposite view, summed up by perhaps his most famous quote: “In the long run we are all dead. Economists set themselves too easy, too useless a task if in tempestuous seasons they can only tell us that when the storm is long past the ocean is flat again.”

By this he meant that the economy had no natural tendency towards full employment. Rather, high unemployment could last indefinitely unless the government was prepared to step in and stimulate demand. This argument formed the centrepiece of his most famous book, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money. The General Theory, as it is commonly known, challenged conventional economic thinking and had a profound influence on policymakers in the decades after the second world war, when it was seen as the responsibility of governments to manage demand to secure full employment.

Keynes saw the many flaws in the capitalist system but was no Marxist. As an unashamed elitist, he saw it as his mission to save capitalism from itself, if only because he saw it as the best way to safeguard civilised values. “He is contemptuous of common men, especially when gathered together in herds,” the social reformer Beatrice Webb once observed. “He dislikes the human herd and has no desire to enlist the human herd on his side.”

Unsurprisingly, the hard left have their suspicions about Keynes. As his biographer Robert Skidelsky wrote: “Marxists have long argued that Keynes’s ideas were taken up because they served the interests of the bourgeoisie in the 1930s and were dropped when they started to endanger capitalist profits in the 1970s.”

It is certainly true that Keynes and his ideas fell out of fashion by the mid-1970s, a period when western economies were afflicted by rising inflation and weak growth at the same time. Postwar Keynesian economists were baffled by the appearance of high inflation and high unemployment at the same time, and the new right – spearheaded politically by Margaret Thatcher and Ronald Reagan – emerged victorious from this era of “stagflation”. Inspired by Hayek’s ideas, it set about dismantling the postwar settlement based on full employment, state ownership, strong trade unions and generous welfare spending.…

items.lbText:
France proposes that EU nations and IEA release oil and diesel from reserves as Iran war drives up cost worldwide

‘Half my day’s pay goes to filling up my car’

British motorists face more pressure at the pumps after the average price of diesel climbed to a record £2 a litre.

The price of a litre at UK forecourts has risen 40.5% since late February, when the US-Israel war on Iran began disrupting supplies of crude and refined oil products from the Gulf, leading to cost increases across the economy.

The RAC motoring group said on Friday that the average price had reached 200.01p a litre, meaning the cost of filling up an average family car is now £110, nearly £32 more than before the Iran war.

Simon Williams, the head of policy at the RAC, said: “This is a pump price threshold that no one wanted to cross.”

The RAC figures measure the average cost of fuel, but in reality many forecourts have been selling diesel above £2 a litre for some time.

Petrol prices are also continuing to rise, with a litre of unleaded costing 174.1p on average, a 31.5% increase since 28 February, taking the cost of a typical tank to £96, just over £23 more than before the US-Iran conflict.

Earlier on Friday the transport minister Keir Mather sought to avert panic at the pumps, insisting the UK was not facing a diesel shortage, after Donald Trump threatened to cut off US supplies of the fuel.

The Trump administration has told Germany and France to release their diesel stockpiles to help ease soaring global energy prices or face a US export ban.

On Thursday, the UK opened talks with European allies over releasing emergency supplies, and Dan Jørgensen, the EU commissioner for energy, said on Friday that Europe was discussing the diesel reserves issue with all members of the International Energy Agency (IEA), not only the US.

In a video conference with G7 leaders, chaired by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, attenders discussed a proposal from the French government that European nations release 50m barrels of diesel from reserve supplies, and for members of the IEA to release 50m barrels of crude oil, Reuters reported.

The UK relies on the US for about 30% of its diesel, with the vast majority coming from mainland Europe, and has reserve supplies for 42 days.

Motorists and small businesses have been struggling with the increasing cost of filling up .

Williams added: “This will be very challenging for households and companies that drive a lot of miles, from commuters, haulage and delivery firms, businesses with large fleets all the way through to sole traders.

“In a cruel twist, it’s diesel vehicles, which were once considered the most cost-effective option for lengthy journeys, that are now burning a hole in people’s pockets.”

Capital Economics estimated that a ban on US exports of diesel could raise UK diesel prices from £2 a litre to £3 a litre and push inflation up to 5%, from 3.1% in August.

The fresh high was recorded after record fuel prices across Europe in recent weeks, which have ignited calls for political leaders to take action to protect consumers against rising cost pressures.

Inflation in the cost of road fuels has outpaced the surge in global oil markets due to a sharp drop in output from refineries damaged by war in the Middle East and in Russia.

Before the Ukraine war, Russia provided between 10% and 15% of the world’s diesel supplies. Another 10% of global diesel supplies transited through the strait of Hormuz from Gulf nations before Iran responded to the US-Israeli attacks by disrupting the strait.

Trump has pushed his Ukrainian counterpart, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, to cease Kyiv’s drone and missile attacks on Russian refineries so they can help to relieve the global fuel squeeze.

The Middle East war has also pushed up household energy bills. This week the quarterly price cap rose by 4%, meaning a typical household in Great Britain will pay £1,723 a year. The cap is forecast to increase by a further 16%, equivalent to adding £276 to the average annual dual-fuel bill, to take it to £1,999, according to the leading forecaster Cornwall Insight.

Reports of talks among European nations to potentially release diesel and oil reserves fuelled a 2.5% fall in the price of Brent crude to $99.78 a barrel.

“This highlights that the main stress in the energy market is no longer crude availability, with Middle East flows recovering,” said Ole Hansen, the head of commodity strategy at Saxo Bank. “But rather refined product supply, constrained by reduced refinery capacity and output across the Middle East and Russia.”

From stag and hen dos to luxury weekends, fans are spending big to create their own version of the hit show

O n Thursday night, the singer-songwriter James Blunt, Love Island host Maya Jama and mathematician Hannah Fry were among the 21 Celebrity Traitors returning to UK screens for another round of deceit and detective work. Famously, contestants do not stay at Ardross Castle in the Scottish Highlands during filming, and the venue is not a hotel, so fans cannot book their own overnight stays without hiring the entire Ross-shire estate. But that has not stopped people from trying to recreate their own versions.

The show’s surging popularity has been accompanied by a bonanza in Traitors-style events across the UK. From stag and hen dos to castle conspiracy weekends, event companies now host year-round imitations for fans looking to recreate the drama of the candle-lit roundtable. The show is also proving to be a boom for the owners of Britain’s crumbling castles – with wealthy fans even hiring them out for their own private events.

“We see a huge spike in people searching for Traitors-style experiences on our pages every time it comes back on TV,” said Roger Masterson, founder of Celtic Castles, which specialises in castle stays and rentals. “We’ve got castle hotels that put together Traitors packages. A 15-bedroom castle might sleep 30, so they’ll bring in couples and organise the faithfuls and traitors over the weekend. They build a story around it and play the game. There are huge varieties with how it’s done.”

Companies organising team bonding exercises are by far the most common customers. GOTO Events, which runs tailored Traitors-style experiences, offers packages from five people to 1,000, complete with their own version of the missions that contestants play to build up the prize pot and a Claudia Winkleman-style host. A GOTO spokesperson said these had become the most popular experience they offer.

“Ever since the show launched, it’s just not died down. We keep thinking things will slow down and they haven’t,” the spokesperson said.

“Everyone pretty much takes it as a bit of fun because you know that someone is lying. In one of my first events, the big boss was one of the betrayers and got called out in the first round. It was funny. Everyone loves calling out their boss.”

But a Traitors-style experience often does not come cheap. Daylong events are a few hundred pounds, while those looking for the full castle experience pay much more. Rothes Glen castle in the Scottish Highlands is offering a three-night package from £4,388 a room for two guests for a castle conspiracy weekend in August next year. A private event will set you back even more: hiring a luxury castle for the weekend can set you back tens of thousands of pounds – and that’s before the cost of organising the game, says Masterson.

“If you were looking at an exclusive-use property, let’s say for 30 people, they might charge £10,000 a night on a bed and breakfast basis. So, a two night stay would be 20 – then add another 10 for the event. You could have an amazing time for £30,000 for the whole weekend,” he says.

The boom is also helping fund repairs to Britain’s crumbling castles, he says. “I’ve been with owners and I ask them why they’re moving into the hospitality market. And they say: ‘Well, we need £100,000 to replace the roof’.”

Since the first episode on Thursday, Traitors mania is set to take over the country once again, running until Friday 30 October. Celebrities will compete for up to £100,000 for their chosen charities.

“We are expecting another surge [with the new series]. We are ready to go,” said GOTO.

items.title: For too long, only the right has expanded the boundaries of what governments can do. Can Burnham change that? | Andy Beckett
items.author: Andy Beckett
items.content:
The PM might come across as a nice bloke but he is politically ruthless. He will need to be if he is to turn big talk into big changes

How much can a Labour government change the country? According to many voters, journalists and politicians, including plenty in the party itself, the answer to that stubbornly recurring question has always been: not that much. Labour governments can’t restructure the economy, radically redistribute wealth, truly empower the disadvantaged or adopt a genuinely ethical foreign policy without upsetting too many powerful interests, from the British rich to the US government to global financial markets.

This endlessly repeated conventional wisdom – internalised by some on the left as well as centrists and the right – has haunted many Labour governments, from the first, tentative ones in the 1920s to Keir Starmer’s diligent but failed administration a century later. Yet conventional wisdom can be wrong, especially in volatile periods such as the current one, when precedent may count for little.

Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

The PM might come across as a nice bloke but he is politically ruthless. He will need to be if he is to turn big talk into big changes

H ow much can a Labour government change the country? According to many voters, journalists and politicians, including plenty in the party itself, the answer to that stubbornly recurring question has always been: not that much. Labour governments can’t restructure the economy, radically redistribute wealth, truly empower the disadvantaged or adopt a genuinely ethical foreign policy without upsetting too many powerful interests, from the British rich to the US government to global financial markets.

This endlessly repeated conventional wisdom – internalised by some on the left as well as centrists and the right – has haunted many Labour governments, from the first, tentative ones in the 1920s to Keir Starmer’s diligent but failed administration a century later. Yet conventional wisdom can be wrong, especially in volatile periods such as the current one, when precedent may count for little.

At last year’s Labour conference, Andy Burnham was widely derided for what was seen as a half-launched and clumsy leadership coup attempt . Much of the media and Starmer’s cabinet reckoned his chances of being prime minister were gone for good. Yet, at this week’s unusually packed and perhaps unwisely optimistic gathering, Burnham’s can-do presence was almost as dominant as Tony Blair’s in his early leadership years: a constant point of reference, from the main hall to the merch stands to leftwing fringe events.

Moreover, Burnham appears to want to use his personal dominance – which may well be briefer than Blair’s, given Labour’s more fragile position in a more fragmented politics – to open up an array of huge issues that his party has long been advised to keep closed. Electoral reform, social care, public intervention in failing privatised utilities, the pension triple lock, even rejoining the EU : announcements about exploring or pursuing all these punctuated his conference speech , in a sequence of softly voiced political shocks.

“Change will be difficult,” he acknowledged. But he insisted: “More of the same isn’t good enough.” At an excited fringe event the night before, his ally Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, who in that job and his previous one as energy secretary has pioneered Labour’s unexpected recent interest in confronting difficult problems and dangerous interests, summed up the party’s defiant new mood. “All politics is a risk. Progressive politics is a particular risk,” he said with relish. Burnham might have similar charisma and communication skills to Blair in the 1990s, but New Labour ministers did not dare say such provocative things.

Defenders of that now remote-seeming political culture would argue that avoiding head-on clashes was one of the reasons Blair was twice re-elected. But Burnham, who served in the Blair government at a formative age, does also have a strong conciliatory impulse, such as his frequently stated keenness to cooperate with other parties. However, as with his reluctance to criticise them by name – his conference speech was almost completely free of the usual party-political attacks – this apparent absence of aggression is in one sense the opposite: a determined attempt to break with the ultra-partisan politics of the post-Brexit decade that has excited many journalists but increasingly exhausted and alienated the public.

Burnham might come across as a nice bloke but he is ruthless, wrongfooting opponents and rendering their tactics obsolete , as his supposedly formidable Labour enemies such as Morgan McSweeney learned this year. Kemi Badenoch and Nigel Farage’s perpetual outrage and tribalism suddenly seem rigid and unreasonable next to Burnham’s talk of hope and national togetherness, and his disarming admission this week that all politicians must do better, that “this country isn’t where any of us would want it to be”.

Labour’s modest but persistent rise in the polls suggests that sufficient voters have had enough of the old high-argument, low-achievement politics to make Labour the leading party again for a period, perhaps up to the next general election and even beyond, when many of his ambitious reforms are actually meant to take place. Of course, proposing, let alone implementing, major changes to the status quo such as loosening the triple lock will also make many voters absolutely furious (even if that policy initially appears popular ), and provide regular targets for Labour’s enemies in Westminster and the media. Yet, with the electorate more divided than ever, and the bar for re-election probably set as low as winning over less than a third of voters, being controversial or unpopular matters less for a government than before – provided it holds its nerve and pleases a large enough core of supporters. Burnham’s sweeping attacks on Labour bogeymen such as the privatised utilities seem likely to achieve that. Meanwhile, his cross-party overtures and support for electoral reform may well lure voters and politicians from the Lib Dems and Greens.

Like Pedro Sánchez in Spain, another centre-left premier of similar age who has managed to stay in power for eight years, Burnham is a paradoxical politician: both frank and evasive; opposed to populism and good at populist gestures; prepared to echo the left’s critique of capitalism but also pro-business; a self-styled lone saviour who is able to work in coalitions. Photogenic and politically agile – you could say shameless – Sánchez and Burnham seem better suited to today’s world of flux, short attention spans and deep discontent than the previous generation of stiff social democrats such as Starmer. Perhaps the modern centre-left is finally working out how to govern and reshape the societies that its more popular 1990s predecessor never sufficiently reformed.…

items.lbText:
People describe their return to physical media – whether to protect data, support artists, or retain control of one’s choices

F or some, it is the security of knowing they have a physical copy of their favourite films and music, free from algorithms, interruptions and the vagaries of streaming. For others, it is the sound of needle on vinyl, the click of a cassette player and the ability to interact with a physical format.

We asked people if they were moving back to CDs, DVDs, vinyl and older formats to escape algorithmically curated content. Here are some of their responses.

Ash, 52, a university lecturer from Cornwall, says he initially embraced streaming but has since tempered that enthusiasm.

“Algorithms make great suggestions, but it feels like you catch a lot of small fish (OK, bands),” he says. “Reading music magazines and artist recommendations and discovering new music for yourself requires more work and effort … it feels like catching the bigger fish.”

Recently, he has returned to buying and listening to physical media. He says he has amassed more than 5,000 records and CDs from 1990 to 2009.

“Technology and streaming felt liberating for a person who has a deep and wide music collection and a bad back. I stopped buying and streamed,” he says, but adds: “I spent more time making playlists than listening to music; I lost the ability to listen to a whole album and missed the physical connection with music.

“I listen to records as an activity, but listen through tech more passively. It’s more like wallpaper than a work of art.”

CJ, 55, a compliance manager from Atlanta, says she decided to return to physical media when shows she liked began disappearing from streaming services.

“HBO removed about 200 episodes of Sesame Street in 2022, so we realised any media we wanted to continue to watch or listen to could be gone, and we’d have no way to get it back,” she says. “As the saying goes, if you can’t hold it, you don’t own it, and we firmly agree with this.

“There are so many shows that aren’t on streaming platforms that we want to rewatch. We scour flea markets and secondhand shops for shows and movies that are hard to find. We have also continued to buy CDs.

“When access to media is so easy to cut off, it makes sense to return to owning what you can, so no one can take it away from you.”

Spotify quickly “bored” Ruth, 67, a retired professor from Michigan, but there were other reasons behind her move to CDs and DVDs.

“Most of all, I wanted to own my music and support the musicians, so I own 5,300 CDs; they have their own walk-in closet,” she says. “Owning my own books, music, and photos (no iCloud) has always seemed normal to me, and, increasingly, prudent.

She adds: “No algorithm is as creative as a well-stocked human brain alive to its actual surroundings.”

Ruth also rents physical film titles by mail from a store in Seattle. “We retired to a rural area with internet unreliable for streaming that wouldn’t sustain a movie without interruptions and buffering. We can stream music from the internet, although even then the connection will conk out every once in a while.”

This summer, Antonio, 40, began buying secondhand CDs from a charity shop in an attempt to get off music subscription services.

“I have a ritual now,” says the software engineer, who lives in Reading. “Twice a month I buy between one and 10 CDs – depending on what is available.

“I decided I didn’t want to rely on a subscription any more and have to deal with price rises, and now I don’t have to share my data – both personal information such as my name, bank account details, location, and my listening history – with a company.

“Nowadays we hand over so much of our data (intentionally or unintentionally) to big corporations that, if I can reduce it in any way, I’m more than happy to do so.”

Quinn, 26, began collecting cassette tapes last year and “quickly fell in love with it”.

He works nights and weekends, leaving him little time to go to concerts. “Buying tapes from bands gave me a way to engage with and support them, despite not being able to see their shows,” says Quinn, who works in food delivery and lives in Washington.

“I really appreciate the format’s restrictions. There’s the routine of interacting with the tape and equipment to play it, the quirks that come with analogue tech and, of course, being able to share music with people by handing them a tape rather than a Spotify link.

“My switch has definitely come with the desire to choose what I’m engaging with. Rather than having content presented to me, I’m seeking it out for myself, or finding it through friends, and that’s a huge part of being low-tech. Sometimes I’m ‘out of the loop’, but I prefer it.”

Tim’s young and adult children all enjoy watching films on older formats.

“In Sweden many people have a summer house,” says the 61-year-old academic, who lives in Stockholm. “Ours, on the mainland, a 45-minute drive from Stockholm, located in the southern end of the Swedish archipelago, contains a video projector from around 2010, a DVD player, and the collection of DVDs watched by my big kids when they were small.

“The biggest luxury for my small kids is when the cables are rigged, the choice of DVD made, and they sit through five minutes of ‘coming soon on Disney’ before we press play on Shrek or whatever the film is.”

Tim says the “aged DVDs” often need a clean, as sticky fingers over the years have left their mark.

“I love this middle stage between the digital and the analogue, and the slowness of the setup to see the films. Next step is to open the trunk containing my (younger) partner’s childhood VHS collection. We’ll see where that goes.”

Sophie, 32, a librarian from Los Angeles, does stream music, but “mostly listens to CDS”. She also often watches DVDs from her own collection or checks them out from the library.…

Most of the betting industry is urging the chancellor not to double slot machine duty to raise up to £460m more a year

Gambling industry kingpins are fuming about reports that the chancellor, John Healey, is considering increasing taxes on high-street slot machines in his first budget.

The influential Social Market Foundation thinktank, the most vocal advocate for a rise in machine games duty (MGD), from 20% to 40%, thinks the measure could raise between £275m and £460m annually , on top of the roughly £610m collected last year.

Its proposal is likely to meet with sympathy from Andy Burnham, a vocal and repeated critic of slot machines , who has already moved to tighten licensing laws so that gambling firms find it harder to open up new shops.

The billionaire owner of Betfred, Fred Done, is among industry bosses who say such a policy would force shop closures, cost jobs and ultimately fail in its objective, depriving the Treasury of taxes.

But not every figure in the gambling world agrees. Stewart Kenny, the co-founder of Paddy Power who has become a critic of his erstwhile industry, accused Done of “scaremongering”.

The Emirati royal is increasingly influential on the world stage. Some see him as a visionary. Others compare him to a Bond villain. Who is he?

On the night of 12 November 1993, a slim, young Brazilian named Royce Gracie stepped into an octagonal cage in Denver, Colorado, and found himself staring up into the eyes of a giant. Gerard Gordeau, a Dutch kickboxer, stood five inches taller, weighed almost three stone more than him, and had an extra decade of fighting experience under his belt. Now the pair were about to engage in bare-knuckle combat: no judges, no separation of opponents by size, no respite until someone either got knocked out cold or begged for mercy.

The fight lasted barely 100 seconds. In that time, Gracie calmly tripped Gordeau up, jumped on his back, and clutched at his throat, forcing the big man to hammer the floor in submission.

About 80,000 pay-per-view spectators watched Gracie’s legendary victory – the finale of the first ever Ultimate Fighting Championship – live on television. Among them was an unassuming business studies student living in San Diego, California. Mesmerised by what he had seen, the student presented himself at a local martial arts academy that specialised in Brazilian jiu-jitsu – the discipline employed by Gracie to humble Gordeau in the cage – and asked to begin lessons. His classmates found it hard to take the newcomer seriously. “I was there the day he showed up,” said Kid Peligro, who went on to become one of the biggest jiu-jitsu stars in the world. “He was wearing shorts, flip-flops and a tank-top; he sat in the corner and barely spoke to anybody.”

The student, who introduced himself as Ben, was in his mid-20s and hailed from the Middle East, but revealed little else about his background. Peligro assumed that he served as the butler or bodyguard to the rich Englishman who sometimes accompanied him to lessons. “Ben was quiet, and he was dedicated,” Peligro told me. “He would often stay behind after class to sweep the mats.” Ben also took physical pain in his stride, even when it involved fractured bones. “If you trained in jiu-jitsu in the 1990s, you were going to get hurt,” said Bobby Razak, a film producer and martial arts enthusiast. “It wasn’t like it is now: very clean, very professional. Back then, it was raw.”

After more than a year of training, Ben made a startling announcement: he was about to return home to Abu Dhabi, capital of the United Arab Emirates, and would be taking the academy’s founder, Nelson Monteiro, along with him. Other invitations soon followed. Rumours spread that Ben was trying to establish his own martial arts centre on the shores of the Persian Gulf. One day, Peligro and his wife were sent a pair of first-class flight tickets to the UAE, worth $24,000 each. When they stepped off the plane, they were astonished to see pictures of a familiar-looking man – clearly Ben’s father – everywhere they turned, from billboards to banknotes. “Ben’s training centre turned out to be one of his family’s palaces,” Peligro said, still marvelling at the memory. “It’s like a fairytale.”

For those trying to uncover the truth behind His Highness Sheikh Tahnoon bin (or “Ben”) Zayed Al Nahyan – royal fixer, reclusive spymaster, financial behemoth – fairytales are nearly all we have to go on. Tahnoon, who really did enrol in Nelson Monteiro’s class under a pseudonym and eventually went on to become a jiu-jitsu black belt in his own right, now sits atop an economic fortune larger than the GDP of several major countries, and is closely entwined both personally and financially with the Trump White House. The global holdings overseen by Tahnoon span windfarms in Scotland and spaceships in Texas, Rihanna’s lingerie line and Richard Caring’s Ivy restaurants. From hospitals to housing blocks, solar farms to ski resorts, there is almost no place on Earth untouched by his financial firepower.

But despite his ever-growing influence on the world stage, Tahnoon prefers to remain in the shadows. He has never given a substantive interview to the press. Those who have worked closely with him are almost always made to sign non-disclosure agreements. Very few people outside the UAE even know his name. “He’s quiet,” says one former US national security official, “and he’s always everywhere.” Sheikh Tahnoon did not respond to an interview request for this article. The UAE foreign ministry did not offer any other senior government figure for interview, and declined to provide any comment.

Tahnoon’s power is soon going to extend over more human lives than ever before. As one of the most important AI financiers on the planet, he is rapidly embedding himself within the infrastructure that will underpin our digital future: its information pipelines and its microchip foundries, its datacentres and the enormous energy plants needed to power and cool them. Some see him as a technological prophet and saviour. Others compare him to a Bond villain. So who is the real “Ben”, and what are his plans for the rest of us?

Anyone trying to find Sheikh Tahnoon must first navigate concentric circles of gatekeepers. These include his closest business associates, as well as a cast of more colourful characters : the former Lebanese prime minister Saad Hariri, for example, or Melissa Moncada, one-time winner of the Miss Globe Colombia beauty pageant, and now a fitness entrepreneur. Even if you get this far, it may not be enough to be granted an audience, and supplicants go to extraordinary lengths to stand out from the crowd.…

Jonathan Liew explains the accusations against Manchester City – and Simon Hattenstone explains how it feels to be a fan

Simon Hattenstone , a features writer for the Guardian, has been a Manchester City fan for more than 50 years. He was very young – and recovering from a childhood illness that had nearly killed him – when he started going to matches in his home town with his dad.

For a long time, it was a relationship built on occasional highs and many, many lows. But then something extraordinary happened: Manchester City’s fortune began to turn and it had a glittering decade – until it all came crashing down.

As the Guardian sports writer Jonathan Liew explains to Annie Kelly, Manchester City has been found guilty of cheating their way to the top, pumping more than £900m of illegal income into the club since 2008. But the story of its catastrophic fall from grace is bigger than just one club, and tells a tale of how the Premier League and the UK have been changed by a huge influx of foreign money.
